entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 6 Am 6:1-14 . Hebrew, "Men designated by name among the first-fruits of the nations," that is, men of note in Israel, the people chosen by God as first of the nations ( Ex 19:5 ; compare Nu 24:20 ) [Piscator]. to whom ... Israel came-- that is, the princes to whom the Israelites used to repair for the decision of controversies, recognizing their authority [Maurer]. I prefer to refer "which" to the antecedent "Zion" and "Samaria"; these were esteemed "chief" strongholds among the heathen nations "to whom ... Israel came" when it entered Canaan; Am 6:2 accords with this.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12592"/><div sID="gen23218" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12592"/>3. Ye persuade yourselves that "the evil day" foretold by the prophets is "far off," though they declare it near (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.22">Eze 12:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.27">27</reference>). Ye in your imagination put it far off, and therefore bring near violent oppression, suffering it to sit enthroned, as it were, among you (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.20">Psa 94:20</reference>). The notion of judgment being far off has always been an incentive to the sinner's recklessness of living (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.12">Ec 8:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.48">Mt 24:48</reference>). Yet that very recklessness brings near the evil day which he puts far off. "Ye bring on fever by your intemperance, and yet would put it far off" [Calvin]. <div eID="gen23218" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12594"/><div sID="gen23223" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12594"/><hi type="bold">5. chant--</hi>literally, "mark distinct sounds and tones."<div eID="gen23223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23224" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">viol--</hi>the lyre, or lute.<div eID="gen23224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">invent ... instruments ... like David--</hi>They fancy they equal David in musical skill (<reference osisRef="1Chr.23.5">1Ch 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.12.36">Ne 12:36</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12599"/><div sID="gen23237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12599"/><hi type="bold">10. a man's uncle--</hi>The nearest relatives had the duty of burying the dead (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.9">Ge 25:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.35.29">35:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.16.31">Jud 16:31</reference>). No nearer relative was left of this man than an uncle.<div eID="gen23237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and he that burneth him--</hi>the uncle, who is also at the same time the one that burneth him (one of the "ten," <reference osisRef="Amos.6.9">Am 6:9</reference>). Burial was the usual Hebrew mode of disposing of their dead. But in cases of necessity, as when the men of Jabesh-gilead took the bodies of Saul and his three sons from the walls of Beth-shan and burned them to save them from being insulted by the Philistines, burning was practised. So in this case, to prevent contagion.<div eID="gen23238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the bones--</hi>that is, the dead body (<reference osisRef="Gen.50.25">Ge 50:25</reference>). Perhaps here there is an allusion in the phrase to the emaciated condition of the body, which was little else but skin and bones.<div eID="gen23239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">say unto him that is by the sides of the house--</hi>that is, to the only one left of the ten in the interior of the house [Maurer] (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Isa.14.13">Is 14:13</reference>).<div eID="gen23240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23241" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hold thy tongue ... we may not ... mention ... the Lord--</hi>After receiving the reply, that none is left besides the one addressed, when the man outside fancies the man still surviving inside to be on the point, as was customary, of expressing devout gratitude to God who spared him, the man outside interrupts him, "Hold thy tongue! for there is not now cause for mentioning with praise (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.7">Jos 23:7</reference>) the name of Jehovah"; for thou also must die; as all the ten are to die to the last man (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.9">Am 6:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Amos.8.3">Am 8:3</reference>). Formerly ye boasted in the name of Jehovah, as if ye were His peculiar people; now ye shall be silent and shudder at His name, as hostile to you, and as one from whom ye wish to be hidden (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">Re 6:16</reference>), [Calvin]. <div eID="gen23241" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 10. a man's uncle-- The nearest relatives had the duty of burying the dead ( Ge 25:9 ; 35:29 ; Jud 16:31 ). No nearer relative was left of this man than an uncle. and he that burneth him-- the uncle, who is also at the same time the one that burneth him (one of the "ten," Am 6:9 ). Burial was the usual Hebrew mode of disposing of their dead. But in cases of necessity, as when the men of Jabesh-gilead took the bodies of Saul and his three sons from the walls of Beth-shan and burned them to save them from being insulted by the Philistines, burning was practised. So in this case, to prevent contagion. the bones-- that is, the dead body ( Ge 50:25 ). Perhaps here there is an allusion in the phrase to the emaciated condition of the body, which was little else but skin and bones. say unto him that is by the sides of the house-- that is, to the only one left of the ten in the interior of the house [Maurer] (compare Note, see on Is 14:13 ). Hold thy tongue ... we may not ... mention ... the Lord-- After receiving the reply, that none is left besides the one addressed, when the man outside fancies the man still surviving inside to be on the point, as was customary, of expressing devout gratitude to God who spared him, the man outside interrupts him, "Hold thy tongue! for there is not now cause for mentioning with praise ( Jos 23:7 ) the name of Jehovah"; for thou also must die; as all the ten are to die to the last man ( Am 6:9 ; compare Am 8:3 ). Formerly ye boasted in the name of Jehovah, as if ye were His peculiar people; now ye shall be silent and shudder at His name, as hostile to you, and as one from whom ye wish to be hidden ( Re 6:16 ), [Calvin].

Hold thy tongue ... we may not ... mention ... the Lord-- After receiving the reply, that none is left besides the one addressed, when the man outside fancies the man still surviving inside to be on the point, as was customary, of expressing devout gratitude to God who spared him, the man outside interrupts him, "Hold thy tongue! for there is not now cause for mentioning with praise ( Jos 23:7 ) the name of Jehovah"; for thou also must die; as all the ten are to die to the last man ( Am 6:9 ; compare Am 8:3 ). Formerly ye boasted in the name of Jehovah, as if ye were His peculiar people; now ye shall be silent and shudder at His name, as hostile to you, and as one from whom ye wish to be hidden ( Re 6:16 ), [Calvin].

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12601"/><div sID="gen23244" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12601"/>12. In turning "judgment (justice) into gall (poison), and ... righteousness into hemlock" (or wormwood, bitter and noxious), ye act as perversely as if one were to make "horses run upon the rock" or to "plough with oxen there" [Maurer]. As horses and oxen are useless on a rock, so ye are incapable of fulfilling justice [Grotius]. Ye impede the course of God's benefits, because ye are as it were a hard rock on which His favor cannot run. "Those that will not be tilled as fields, shall be abandoned as rocks" [Calvin]. <div eID="gen23244" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12603"/><div sID="gen23247" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12603"/><hi type="bold">14. from the entering in of Hamath--</hi>the point of entrance for an invading army (as Assyria) into Israel from the north; specified here, as Hamath had been just before subjugated by Jeroboam II (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.2">Am 6:2</reference>). Do not glory in your recently acquired city, for it shall be the starting-point for the foe to afflict you. How sad the contrast to the feast of Solomon attended by a congregation from this same Hamath, the most northern boundary of Israel, to the Nile, the river of Egypt, the most southern boundary!<div eID="gen23247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23248" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the river of the wilderness--</hi>that is, to Kedron, which empties itself into the north bay of the Dead Sea below Jericho (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.15">2Ch 28:15</reference>), the southern boundary of the ten tribes (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2Ki 14:25</reference>, "from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain") [Maurer]. If this verse includes Judah, as well as Israel (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>, "Zion" and "Samaria"), Grotius' view is correct; and it agrees with <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.65">1Ki 8:65</reference>. <chapter eID="Amos.6"/>
